stances.claim: In July 1995, when Art had finally convinced himself that the chapter was closed, the past returned quietly, almost apologetically -- a friend from the Supreme Court approached him without ceremony, without persuasion, without urgency: 'Why don't you try again? There won't be another vacancy for years.' The words were simple. The effect was not.

stances.claim: Art dismissed the suggestion almost immediately -- he had already surrendered; he had prayed not for appointment but for detachment; he had offered up the ambition itself, believing that obedience meant letting go. To hope again felt like disobedience; to apply again felt like pride disguised as perseverance. And yet -- the words lingered.

stances.claim: On the night of July 29, 1995, sleep refused him; past midnight he lay awake, staring into the darkness, rehearsing the same question over and over with the intensity of a cross-examination: Was he clinging to ambition? Or resisting obedience? He rose and prayed -- not briefly, not casually -- for hours; he asked only for clarity, for the grace to know whether persistence would be faithfulness or defiance.

stances.claim: The following morning, Sunday, he served as a Special Minister of Holy Communion; then the Gospel was read -- from Luke: 'Ask and you shall receive. Seek and you shall find. Knock and the door shall be opened to you.' The effect was immediate and physical -- his skin prickled, cold sweat gathered at his temples, gooseflesh rose along his arms; the words did not sound ancient -- they sounded personal, uncomfortably so. He whispered inwardly, almost in protest: 'My Lord, is this meant for me?'

stances.claim: But discipline had taught him caution -- he prayed again that day: 'If this is truly Your will, give me another sign. One more. I do not want to be deceived by my own longing.' One week later, in the same church, with the same priest, the Gospel was read again -- this time the Transfiguration: 'A cloud came and overshadowed them... and a voice said: This is my Son, my Chosen One. Listen to Him.' Listen. The word struck him harder than the first reading. Not ask. Not seek. Not knock. Listen. In that single command, the conflict resolved itself -- listening did not mean ambition, it meant obedience; it meant acting not because he wanted to rise, but because he was being called to respond.

stances.claim: He submitted his name to the Judicial and Bar Council once more -- the resistance returned immediately; at one meeting there was a concerted effort to strike his name from the list; old objections resurfaced; familiar skepticism hardened; the vote came dangerously close. Only one member intervened -- 'Let us defer this. We are meeting again next week.' It was a procedural delay. Nothing more. Two days later, the same member spoke to him privately: 'Unless something extraordinary happens, you will be removed next week.' Unless a miracle happens.

stances.claim: Art did not panic -- he prayed not defensively, not anxiously, but defiantly in faith; he had reached a strange calm; he no longer argued his merits, he no longer rehearsed rebuttals; he rested entirely on a conviction that had crystallized: human forces, however exalted, could not override divine will. At the next meeting, something inexplicable occurred -- no one objected, the accusations did not resurface, the arguments did not return, the opposition did not speak. Silence filled the room. For the first time in three years, his name survived the screening. There was no applause, no announcement, no sense of triumph -- only a quiet, unmistakable knowing. The miracle had arrived -- not with thunder, but with stillness. And the door, at last, had opened.

one_paragraph_summary: Art's most-intimate spiritual chapter, the bridge between seven JBC rejections and the Supreme Court appointment. In July 1995, after Art had convinced himself the chapter was closed, a friend from the Supreme Court approached him 'without ceremony, without persuasion, without urgency': 'Why don't you try again? There won't be another vacancy for years.' Art dismissed the suggestion -- to hope again felt like disobedience, to apply again felt like pride disguised as perseverance -- yet the words lingered. On the night of July 29, 1995, sleep refused him; past midnight he cross-examined himself: was he clinging to ambition, or resisting obedience? He rose and prayed for hours, asking only for clarity. The following Sunday, serving as Special Minister of Holy Communion, the Gospel was read from Luke: 'Ask and you shall receive. Seek and you shall find. Knock and the door shall be opened to you.' His skin prickled, cold sweat gathered, gooseflesh rose -- the words sounded 'uncomfortably' personal. Wary of mistaking 'desire for discernment,' he asked for another sign: 'I do not want to be deceived by my own longing.' One week later, in the same church with the same priest, the Gospel was the Transfiguration: 'This is my Son, my Chosen One. Listen to Him.' Listen -- 'not ask, not seek, not knock' -- and the conflict resolved itself: 'listening did not mean ambition. It meant obedience.' He resubmitted his name to the JBC; resistance returned, the vote came dangerously close to striking him, and one member intervened to defer the meeting one week. Two days later that same member warned privately: 'Unless something extraordinary happens, you will be removed next week.' Unless a miracle happens. Art did not panic; he prayed 'defiantly in faith,' resting on the conviction that 'human forces, however exalted, could not override divine will.' At the next meeting, 'no one objected, the accusations did not resurface, the arguments did not return, the opposition did not speak. Silence filled the room.' For the first time in three years his name survived -- 'no applause, no announcement, no sense of triumph,' only 'a quiet, unmistakable knowing.' Closing: 'The miracle had arrived -- not with thunder, but with stillness. And the door, at last, had opened.'
